This document describes the various file formats used in VerMoUTH and Martinize2. VerMoUTH supports several input and output file formats for representing molecular structures, force fields, and mappings between different force field resolutions. Understanding these file formats is crucial for effectively using the system and creating custom force fields or mappings.

## Overview of File Formats

VerMoUTH utilizes several types of files that serve different purposes in the molecular topology generation workflow:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Input Structure Files"
        PDB["PDB Files (.pdb)"]
        GRO["GRO Files (.gro)"]
        CIF["CIF Files (.cif)"]
    end

    subgraph "Force Field Definition Files"
        FF["Force Field Files (.ff)"]
        ITP["GROMACS Topology Files (.itp)"]
    end

    subgraph "Mapping Files"
        MAP["Mapping Files (.map)"]
        MAPPING["Modification Mappings (.mapping)"]
    end

    subgraph "Output Files"
        TOP["Topology Files (.top)"]
        CGPDB["Coarse-Grained PDB (.pdb)"]
        ITP_OUT["ITP Fragments (.itp)"]
    end

    PDB --> Reader
    GRO --> Reader
    CIF --> Reader
    
    Reader --> Molecule
    
    FF --> FFDirector
    ITP --> ITPDirector
    
    FFDirector --> ForceField
    ITPDirector --> ForceField
    
    MAP --> MappingDirector
    MAPPING --> MappingDirector
    
    MappingDirector --> MappingObject
    
    ForceField --> ProcessingPipeline
    Molecule --> ProcessingPipeline
    MappingObject --> ProcessingPipeline
    
    ProcessingPipeline --> TOP
    ProcessingPipeline --> CGPDB
    ProcessingPipeline --> ITP_OUT
    
    class Reader,FFDirector,ITPDirector,MappingDirector,ProcessingPipeline,ForceField,Molecule,MappingObject nodes
```

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:15-23](), [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:15-18](), [vermouth/map_input.py:17-19](), [doc/source/file_formats.rst:1-36]()

## 1. Force Field Files (.ff)

Force field (.ff) files describe molecule components for a given force field. These files use a format similar to GROMACS topology files but with additional sections specific to VerMoUTH's needs.

### File Structure and Directives

A force field file consists of multiple sections, each introduced by a directive enclosed in square brackets. The main top-level directives are:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Force Field File Structure"
        FF["Force Field (.ff)"]
        FF --> Variables["[variables]"]
        FF --> Macros["[macros]"]
        FF --> Citations["[citations]"]
        FF --> Molecules["[moleculetype]"]
        FF --> Links["[link]"]
        FF --> Mods["[modification]"]
        
        Molecules --> Atoms["[atoms]"]
        Molecules --> Bonds["[bonds]/[angles]/etc."]
        Molecules --> Edges["[edges]"]
        Molecules --> Meta["[meta]"]
        
        Links --> LinkAtoms["[atoms]"]
        Links --> Patterns["[patterns]"]
        Links --> Features["[features]"]
        Links --> LinkBonds["[bonds]/[angles]/etc."]
        Links --> MolMeta["[molmeta]"]
        
        Mods --> ModAtoms["[atoms]"]
        Mods --> ModPatterns["[patterns]"]
        Mods --> ModFeatures["[features]"]
        Mods --> ModInter["[bonds]/[angles]/etc."]
    end
```

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:63-91](), [doc/source/file_formats.rst:37-162]()

#### Major Directives in .ff Files

| Directive | Purpose | Required | Example |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------|
| `[macros]` | Defines substitution patterns to be used throughout the file | No | `prot_default_bb_type P2` |
| `[variables]` | Defines force field-wide parameters | No | `elastic_network_bond_type 1` |
| `[citations]` | References to publications for the force field | No | `Martini3` |
| `[moleculetype]` | Defines a block (residue/molecule template) | No | `ALA 3` (name + exclusion number) |
| `[link]` | Defines connections between blocks | No | `resname "ALA"` |
| `[modification]` | Defines modifications to blocks | No | `PTM-name` |

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:44-162](), [vermouth/ffinput.py:95-106]()

#### Moleculetype Sub-directives

| Sub-directive | Purpose | Required | Example |
|---------------|---------|----------|---------|
| `[atoms]` | Lists atoms with properties | Yes | `1 P5 1 GLY BB 1 0 47` |
| `[edges]` | Explicitly adds edges to the molecular graph | No | `BB SC1` |
| `[bonds]` | Defines bond interactions | No | `BB SC1 1 0.47 5000` |
| `[angles]` | Defines angle interactions | No | `BB SC1 SC2 2 100 20` |
| `[dihedrals]` | Defines dihedral interactions | No | `BB SC1 SC2 SC3 1 -30 5 1` |
| `[constraints]` | Defines distance constraints | No | `BB SC1 1 0.47` |
| `[meta]` | Block-specific metadata | No | `flag key1 0.15` |

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:163-256](), [vermouth/ffinput.py:221-225]()

#### Link Sub-directives

| Sub-directive | Purpose | Required | Example |
|---------------|---------|----------|---------|
| `[atoms]` | Specifies or modifies atom attributes | No | `BB {"resname": "ALA"}` |
| `[patterns]` | Specifies patterns to match | No | `BB +BB` |
| `[features]` | Lists features provided by the link | No | `scfix` |
| `[molmeta]` | Metadata to be added to the molecule | No | `category protein` |
| `[edges]` | Specifies edges that should exist | No | `BB SC1` |
| `[non-edges]` | Specifies edges that should not exist | No | `BB SC2` |

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:257-351](), [vermouth/ffinput.py:432-466]()

#### Modification Sub-directives

| Sub-directive | Purpose | Required | Example |
|---------------|---------|----------|---------|
| `[atoms]` | Lists atoms to be modified or added | Yes | `C1 {"PTM_atom": true, "element": "C"}` |
| `[bonds]` (and other interactions) | Interactions to add | No | `BB PTM-C1 1 0.33 7500` |

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:354-369](), [vermouth/ffinput.py:446-462]()

### Special Metadata Syntax

The force field file format allows for special metadata annotations using JSON-style attributes. These can be used to:

1. Group interactions with the `group` attribute
2. Add conditional interactions with `ifdef`/`ifndef` attributes 
3. Add comments to interactions
4. Control parameter versioning

Example:
```
[bonds]
#meta {"group": "Side chain bonds", "ifdef": "FLEXIBLE"}
BB SC1  1 0.47 5000
```

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:375-407](), [vermouth/ffinput.py:360-376]()

## 2. Mapping Files (.map & .mapping)

Mapping files define how to convert molecular structures between different force field resolutions, such as from atomistic to coarse-grained (forward mapping) or vice versa (backward mapping).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Mapping Process"
        MAPFile["Mapping File (.map/.mapping)"]
        FROM["Source ForceField"]
        TO["Target ForceField"]
        BLOCK1["Source Block"]
        BLOCK2["Target Block"]
        MAPPING["Mapping Object"]
        
        MAPFile --> MappingDirector
        FROM --> MappingDirector
        TO --> MappingDirector
        
        MappingDirector --> MAPPING
        
        BLOCK1 --> MAPPING
        BLOCK2 --> MAPPING
        
        MAPPING --> |"Used by DoMapping"| TRANSFORMATION["Resolution Transformation"]
    end
```

Sources: [vermouth/map_input.py:17-19](), [vermouth/map_parser.py:16-17](), [vermouth/processors/do_mapping.py:16-19]()

### .map File Format

The `.map` file format is used primarily for basic block-to-block mappings. Originally developed for the backward program, it specifies how atoms in one force field correspond to beads in another.

#### Directives in .map Files

| Directive | Purpose | Required | Example |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------|
| `[molecule]` | Name of the residue being mapped | Yes | `ALA` |
| `[from]` | Source force field name | Yes | `universal` |
| `[to]` | Target force field name | Yes | `martini22` |
| `[martini]` | Lists all target beads | Yes | `BB SC1` |
| `[atoms]` | Maps source atoms to target beads | Yes | `1 N BB` |

Example:
```
[molecule]
ALA

[martini]
BB SC1

[atoms]
1 N BB
2 H BB
3 CA BB
4 HA BB
5 CB SC1
6 HB1 SC1
7 HB2 SC1
8 HB3 SC1
9 C BB
10 O BB
```

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:411-486](), [vermouth/map_input.py:36-40]()

### .mapping File Format

The `.mapping` file format is an extension of the `.map` format, designed specifically for mapping modifications between force fields.

#### Directives in .mapping Files

| Directive | Purpose | Required | Example |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------|
| `[modification]` | Marks start of modification mapping | Yes | _(empty)_ |
| `[from]` | Source force field name | Yes | `amber` |
| `[to]` | Target force field name | Yes | `martini3001` |
| `[from blocks]` | Modification name in source | Yes | `PHOSPHORYLATED` |
| `[to blocks]` | Modification name in target | Yes | `PHOSPHORYLATED` |
| `[from nodes]` | Additional source nodes | No | `P {"atomname": "P", "atype": "P"}` |
| `[to nodes]` | Additional target nodes | No | `PO4 {"atomname": "PO4", "atype": "Qa"}` |

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:504-527](), [vermouth/map_parser.py:581-630]()

## 3. GROMACS Topology Files (.itp)

GROMACS topology (.itp) files are read by VerMoUTH to define blocks. This allows direct use of GROMACS topologies as sources for force field definitions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "ITP File Processing"
        ITP["ITP File (.itp)"]
        ITPDir["ITPDirector"]
        FF["ForceField"]
        Block1["Block"]
        Block2["Block"]
        
        ITP --> ITPDir
        ITPDir --> FF
        FF --> Block1
        FF --> Block2
    end
```

Sources: [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:15-18](), [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-27]()

### ITP File Structure

The ITP file format is based on the GROMACS topology format, with sections for molecule types, atoms, and various interaction types.

#### Main Sections in ITP Files

| Section | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `[moleculetype]` | Defines a molecule/residue with exclusion number | `GLY 3` |
| `[atoms]` | Lists atoms with properties | `1 P4 1 ALA BB 1` |
| `[bonds]` | Lists bond interactions | `1 2 1 0.33 1000` |
| `[angles]` | Lists angle interactions | `1 2 3 2 130 25` |
| `[dihedrals]` | Lists dihedral and improper interactions | `1 2 3 4 1 180 10 1` |
| `[constraints]` | Lists distance constraints | `1 2 1 0.33` |

ITP files can also include preprocessor macros like `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#else`, and `#endif`, which are processed by the ITP reader.

Sources: [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:25-48](), [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:237-246]()

### Key Differences Between .ff and .itp Files

While both .ff and .itp files describe molecular components, there are some important differences:

1. **.ff files**:
   - Support more VerMoUTH-specific features (links, modifications)
   - Use atom names as node identifiers
   - Allow for JSON-style attributes
   - Include mapping-related directives

2. **.itp files**:
   - Use numerical indices for atom references
   - Strictly follow GROMACS syntax
   - Support GROMACS preprocessor directives (`#ifdef`, etc.)
   - Don't support link and modification definitions

Sources: [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-30](), [vermouth/ffinput.py:63-91]()

## 4. Relationship Between File Formats and System Components

The following diagram illustrates how the different file formats interact with the core data structures in VerMoUTH:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ForceField {
        +name: str
        +blocks: dict
        +links: list
        +modifications: dict
        +features: set
    }
    
    class Block {
        +name: str
        +nrexcl: int
        +nodes: dict
        +edges: list
        +interactions: dict
    }
    
    class Link {
        +nodes: dict
        +edges: list
        +interactions: dict
        +patterns: list
        +features: list
    }
    
    class Modification {
        +name: str
        +nodes: dict
        +edges: list
        +interactions: dict
    }
    
    class Mapping {
        +block_from: Graph
        +block_to: Block
        +mapping: dict
        +references: dict
        +type: str
    }
    
    class FFDirector {
        +force_field: ForceField
        +parse(lines)
    }
    
    class ITPDirector {
        +force_field: ForceField
        +parse(lines)
    }
    
    class MappingDirector {
        +force_fields: dict
        +parse(lines)
    }
    
    FFFile --|> FFDirector: parses
    ITPFile --|> ITPDirector: parses
    MAPFile --|> MappingDirector: parses
    
    FFDirector --> ForceField: populates
    ITPDirector --> ForceField: populates
    MappingDirector --> Mapping: creates
    
    ForceField o-- Block: contains
    ForceField o-- Link: contains
    ForceField o-- Modification: contains
    
    Mapping --> Block: references
```

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:62-91](), [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-36](), [vermouth/map_parser.py:31-117]()

## 5. Processing Pipeline and File Formats

The following diagram shows how file formats fit into the Martinize2 processing pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Input Files"
        PDB[".pdb File"]
        GRO[".gro File"]
        CIF[".cif File"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Force Field Files"
        FF[".ff Files"]
        ITP[".itp Files"]
        MAP[".map/.mapping Files"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing Pipeline"
        Read["1. PDBInput/GROInput/CIFInput"]
        MakeBonds["2. MakeBonds"]
        Repair["3. RepairGraph"]
        Canonicalize["4. CanonicalizeModifications"]
        DoMapping["5. DoMapping"]
        DoLinks["6. DoLinks"]
        Elastic["7. ApplyRubberBand"]
        Write["8. Write Topology"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Files"
        TOP[".top File"]
        OUTPDB[".pdb File"]
        OUTITP[".itp File"]
    end
    
    PDB --> Read
    GRO --> Read
    CIF --> Read
    
    FF --> ForceField
    ITP --> ForceField
    MAP --> Mappings
    
    ForceField --> DoLinks
    ForceField --> Repair
    Mappings --> DoMapping
    
    Read --> MakeBonds
    MakeBonds --> Repair
    Repair --> Canonicalize
    Canonicalize --> DoMapping
    DoMapping --> DoLinks
    DoLinks --> Elastic
    Elastic --> Write
    
    Write --> TOP
    Write --> OUTPDB
    Write --> OUTITP
```

Sources: [doc/source/martinize2_workflow.rst:1-36]()

## Summary

The file formats used in VerMoUTH and Martinize2 are designed to support flexible descriptions of molecular structures, force fields, and the mappings between them. The key formats are:

1. **Force field files (.ff)**: Define blocks, links, and modifications for a force field
2. **Mapping files (.map, .mapping)**: Define transformations between force fields
3. **GROMACS topology files (.itp)**: Provide standard GROMACS topology definitions
4. **Structure files (.pdb, .gro, .cif)**: Provide input molecular structures

Understanding these file formats is essential for creating custom force fields, defining new mappings between resolutions, and efficiently using the VerMoUTH/Martinize2 system for molecular simulations.

Sources: [doc/source/file_formats.rst:1-36](), [doc/source/data.rst:1-115]()

This page explains how to create and use custom force fields in the vermouth-martinize framework. Custom force fields allow you to define your own molecular building blocks, interactions, and modifications for coarse-grained simulations. For information about using the built-in force fields provided with the package, see [Force Fields](#2.2).

## Overview of Force Field Structure

In vermouth-martinize, a force field is represented by the `ForceField` class, which contains several key components:

```mermaid
graph TD
    FF["ForceField"] --> Blocks
    FF --> Links
    FF --> Modifications
    FF --> Variables
    FF --> Citations
    
    Blocks --> Block1["Block (e.g., amino acid)"]
    Blocks --> Block2["Block (e.g., lipid)"]
    
    Links --> Link1["Link (e.g., peptide bond)"]
    Links --> Link2["Link (e.g., disulfide)"]
    
    Modifications --> Mod1["Modification (e.g., phosphorylation)"]
    Modifications --> Mod2["Modification (e.g., glycosylation)"]
    
    Block1 --> BlockAtoms["Atoms"]
    Block1 --> BlockInteractions["Interactions (bonds, angles, etc.)"]
    
    Link1 --> LinkPatterns["Patterns (matching rules)"]
    Link1 --> LinkFeatures["Features (properties)"]
    Link1 --> LinkAtoms["Atoms"]
    Link1 --> LinkInteractions["Interactions"]
    
    Mod1 --> ModAtoms["Atoms"]
    Mod1 --> ModInteractions["Interactions"]
```

Sources: [vermouth/forcefield.py:35-82](vermouth/forcefield.py:35-82), [vermouth/molecule.py](vermouth/molecule.py)

## Force Field File Formats

Vermouth-martinize supports two main file formats for defining force fields:

1. **FF Files** (`.ff`): A custom format for defining all force field components
2. **ITP Files** (`.itp`): GROMACS topology files that can define molecular building blocks

### File Parsing Process

```mermaid
graph TD
    FFFiles[".ff Files"] --> FFDirector["FFDirector"]
    ITPFiles[".itp Files"] --> ITPDirector["ITPDirector"]
    
    FFDirector --> ParseBlocks["Parse Blocks"]
    FFDirector --> ParseLinks["Parse Links"]
    FFDirector --> ParseModifications["Parse Modifications"]
    FFDirector --> ParseVariables["Parse Variables"]
    
    ITPDirector --> ParseITPBlocks["Parse Blocks"]
    
    ParseBlocks --> ForceField["ForceField"]
    ParseLinks --> ForceField
    ParseModifications --> ForceField
    ParseVariables --> ForceField
    ParseITPBlocks --> ForceField
```

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:63-147](vermouth/ffinput.py:63-147), [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-479](vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-479)

## Creating Custom Force Fields with FF Files

The `.ff` file format is the preferred method for creating custom force fields as it supports all components. Force field files use sections indicated by square brackets (`[ section_name ]`) to define different components.

### Variables Section

Variables can be defined and used throughout the force field:

```
[ variables ]
elastic_network_bond_type 1
res_min_dist 3
prot_default_bb_type P2
```

Variables are referenced using the `$` prefix:

```
[ atoms ]
1   $prot_default_bb_type   1   LEU   BB   1   0
```

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:207-213](vermouth/ffinput.py:207-213)

### Blocks

Blocks represent molecular building blocks like amino acids or lipids. They are defined using the `moleculetype` section followed by atoms and interactions:

```
[ moleculetype ]
; molname   nrexcl
ALA         1

[ atoms ]
;id type resnr residu atom cgnr  charge
1   P4   1     ALA    BB   1     0
2   C3   1     ALA    SC1  2     0

[ bonds ]
;  i   j  funct   length  force.c.
   1   2  1       0.270   7500
```

The `atoms` section defines each atom with:
- ID: Atom identifier (numeric or name)
- Type: Atom type (determines interactions)
- Resnr: Residue number
- Residu: Residue name
- Atom: Atom name
- Cgnr: Charge group
- Charge: Electric charge

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:215-231](vermouth/ffinput.py:215-231), [vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/aminoacids.ff:30-57](vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/aminoacids.ff:30-57)

### Interactions

Blocks and links can define various types of interactions:

```
[ bonds ]
;  i   j  funct   length  force.c.
   1   2  1       0.270   7500

[ angles ]
;  i   j   k  funct   angle  force.c.
   1   2   3  2       120.0  50.0

[ dihedrals ]
;  i   j   k   l  funct   angle  force.c.
   1   2   3   4  1       180.0  10.0
```

Supported interaction types include:
- `bonds`: Covalent bonds
- `angles`: Bond angles
- `dihedrals`: Proper dihedral angles
- `impropers`: Improper dihedral angles
- `constraints`: Distance constraints
- `pairs`: Non-bonded pairs
- `exclusions`: Excluded interactions

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:274-421](vermouth/ffinput.py:274-421)

### Links

Links define connections between blocks, such as peptide bonds in proteins:

```
[ link ]
[ atoms ]
;atom1 atom2     resname atom  cgnr  charge
 BB    +BB       *       BB    1     0

[ bonds ]
;atom1 atom2  funct  length  force.c.
 BB    +BB    1      0.350   1250

[ angles ]
;atom1 atom2 atom3  funct  angle  force.c.
 -BB   BB    +BB    2      134    25
```

In links, atom names can be prefixed to indicate relative positions:
- `+`: Next residue (e.g., `+BB`)
- `-`: Previous residue (e.g., `-BB`)
- `>`, `<`: Other ordering relationships

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:431-465](vermouth/ffinput.py:431-465), [vermouth/data/force_fields/martini22/aminoacids.ff:593-603](vermouth/data/force_fields/martini22/aminoacids.ff:593-603)

### Patterns and Features

Links can include patterns to specify when they should be applied:

```
[ link ]
[ patterns ]
; Apply to residues with names in protein_resnames
resname $protein_resnames

[ features ]
; Define features provided by this link
protein_backbone
```

The `patterns` section defines conditions for matching blocks, while the `features` section defines properties provided by the link.

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:453-465](vermouth/ffinput.py:453-465)

### Modifications

Modifications define chemical changes to blocks, such as phosphorylation:

```
[ modification ]
SER-P  ; Phosphorylated serine

[ atoms ]
;id  type resnr residu atom cgnr   charge
 BB   P5   1     SER    BB   1      0
 SC1  P1   1     SER    SC1  2      0
 P1   Qa   1     SER-P  P    3     -1.0

[ bonds ]
;  i   j  funct   length  force.c.
  SC1  P1  1       0.28    7500
```

Sources: [vermouth/ffinput.py:437-451](vermouth/ffinput.py:437-451)

## Creating Custom Force Fields with ITP Files

ITP files can also be used to define blocks, though they have limitations compared to FF files. The syntax is similar but with some differences:

```
[ moleculetype ]
; molname   nrexcl
ALA         1

[ atoms ]
;id type resnr residu atom cgnr  charge mass
1   P4   1     ALA    BB   1     0     72
2   C3   1     ALA    SC1  2     0     45

[ bonds ]
;  i   j  funct   length  force.c.
   1   2  1       0.270   7500
```

Key differences compared to FF files:
- ITP files use numeric indices (1-based) for atoms in interactions
- ITP files cannot define links or modifications
- ITP files may include additional parameters like mass

Sources: [vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-266](vermouth/gmx/itp_read.py:24-266)

## Example Force Field Files

Below is a simplified example of a force field definition for alanine residue:

```
[ variables ]
prot_default_bb_type P2
stiff_fc 1000000

[ moleculetype ]
; molname       nrexcl
ALA                1

[ atoms ]
;id type resnr residu atom cgnr   charge
 1   SP2    1   ALA    BB     1      0
 2   TC3    1   ALA    SC1    2      0 

[ constraints ]
#meta {"group": "Side chain bonds", "ifndef": "FLEXIBLE"}
;  i     j   funct   length  
  BB   SC1    1       0.270

[ bonds ]
#meta {"group": "Side chain bonds", "ifdef": "FLEXIBLE"}
;  i     j   funct   length  
  BB   SC1    1       0.270  $stiff_fc
```

This example defines alanine with a backbone bead (BB) and a side chain bead (SC1) connected by either a constraint or a stiff bond depending on whether the "FLEXIBLE" flag is defined.

Sources: [vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/aminoacids.ff:30-57](vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/aminoacids.ff:30-57)

## Loading and Using Custom Force Fields

To use a custom force field, you need to create a `ForceField` object and load your force field files:

```python
from vermouth.forcefield import ForceField

# Method 1: Load from a directory
force_field = ForceField(directory='path/to/force_field_directory')

# Method 2: Create empty and load manually
force_field = ForceField(name='my_custom_ff')
force_field.read_from('path/to/force_field_directory')

# Method 3: Find force fields in a directory
from vermouth.forcefield import find_force_fields
force_fields = find_force_fields('path/to/force_fields_directory')
```

The force field directory should contain one or more `.ff` or `.itp` files. Conventionally, each force field is organized in its own directory, with the directory name matching the force field name.

Sources: [vermouth/forcefield.py:63-147](vermouth/forcefield.py:63-147), [vermouth/forcefield.py:143-189](vermouth/forcefield.py:143-189)

## Force Field Directory Structure

A typical force field directory structure might look like:

```
my_custom_ff/
├── aminoacids.ff    # Amino acid definitions
├── lipids.ff        # Lipid definitions
├── general.ff       # General parameters
└── citations.bib    # Literature references
```

The force field files are processed in alphabetical order, so you may want to use prefixes to control the loading order if certain definitions depend on others.

Sources: [vermouth/forcefield.py:192-199](vermouth/forcefield.py:192-199)

## Force Field Validation

When creating a custom force field, it's important to validate your definitions to ensure they're correctly formatted and produce the expected results. Common issues to check for include:

1. Missing or invalid parameters
2. Inconsistent atom naming
3. Improper interaction definitions
4. Invalid syntax or undefined variables

You can test your force field by loading it and building simple molecules to ensure the topology is generated as expected.

## Best Practices

1. **Use organization**: Separate different molecule types into different files
2. **Be consistent**: Use consistent naming conventions for atom types
3. **Document extensively**: Add comments to explain the purpose of definitions
4. **Use variables**: Define common parameters as variables for easier maintenance
5. **Include citations**: Reference the sources used for parameters

By following these guidelines, you can create robust and maintainable custom force fields for your simulations.

Sources: [vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/aminoacids.ff](vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/aminoacids.ff), [vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/general.ff](vermouth/data/force_fields/martini3001/general.ff)

# Development Guide

<details>

This guide provides essential information for developers who want to contribute to the vermouth-martinize project. It covers setting up a development environment, understanding the project structure, following coding standards, writing tests, and navigating the continuous integration and deployment pipeline. For specific information about the CI/CD pipeline and testing framework, see [CI/CD Pipeline](#4.3.1) and [Testing Framework](#4.3.2).

## 1. Project Overview

Vermouth-martinize is a Python-based project that consists of:
- The `vermouth` library: A versatile, modular transformation helper for molecular structures
- The `martinize2` command-line tool: A program that uses vermouth to convert atomistic structures to coarse-grained representations

The project follows modern Python development practices with a comprehensive test suite, automated CI/CD pipeline, and standardized code quality checks.

Sources: [README.md:1-19]()

## 2. Setting Up a Development Environment

### 2.1 Prerequisites

- Python 3.9 or greater
- Git
- (Optional) DSSP for secondary structure determination

### 2.2 Development Installation

1. Clone the repository:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/marrink-lab/vermouth-martinize.git
   cd vermouth-martinize
   ```

2. Install in development mode:
   ```bash
   pip install -e .
   ```

3. Install development requirements:
   ```bash
   pip install -r requirements-tests.txt  # Testing dependencies
   pip install -r requirements-docs.txt   # Documentation dependencies
   ```

Sources: [setup.cfg:17-24](), [README.md:30-51]()

### 2.3 Project Structure

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Core Package Structure"
        Vermouth["vermouth (library)"]
        Martinize["martinize2 (CLI tool)"]
        
        Vermouth --> DataStructures["Data Structures\n(Molecule, ForceField, etc.)"]
        Vermouth --> Processors["Processors\n(Graph transformations)"]
        Vermouth --> IO["File I/O\n(PDB, GRO, ITP readers)"]
        Vermouth --> FF["Force Field Definitions"]
        
        Martinize --> CLI["Command-line Interface"]
        Martinize --> Pipeline["Processing Pipeline"]
        
        CLI --> Vermouth
        Pipeline --> Processors
    end
    
    subgraph "Development Files"
        Tests["Tests\n(/vermouth/tests)"]
        Docs["Documentation\n(/doc/source)"]
        Setup["Setup Files\n(setup.py, setup.cfg)"]
        CI["CI/CD Configuration\n(.github/workflows)"]
    end
```

Sources: [setup.py:14-30]()

## 3. Development Workflow

### 3.1 Making Changes

1. Create a feature branch from `master`
2. Make your changes
3. Add tests that cover your changes
4. Ensure all tests pass with `pytest -vv`
5. Ensure code meets quality standards with `pylint`
6. Submit a pull request to the `master` branch

### 3.2 Code Style Guidelines

The project uses `pylint` for code quality enforcement with the following thresholds:

- Library code (vermouth): minimum score 8.0
- Command-line tool (martinize2): minimum score 9.0

```bash
# Run pylint checks
pylint --disable=fixme --fail-under=8.0 vermouth
pylint --disable=fixme --fail-under=9.0 bin/martinize2
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:88-91]()

### 3.3 Documentation

Documentation is built using Sphinx. New code should include proper docstrings following the project's conventions.

To build documentation locally:

```bash
mkdir -p doc/source/_static
sphinx-build -EnW -b html doc/source/ doc/build/html
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:114-117]()

## 4. Testing Framework

The project uses pytest for testing, with hypothesis for property-based testing. Coverage is tracked to ensure comprehensive test coverage.

### 4.1 Running Tests

```bash
# Run all tests
pytest -vv

# Run with coverage
coverage run $(which pytest) -vv
coverage report
```

### 4.2 Writing Tests

Tests should be placed in the `vermouth/tests` directory. The project uses a combination of unit tests, integration tests, and property-based tests.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Testing Structure"
        PyTest["pytest Test Runner"]
        
        PyTest --> UnitTests["Unit Tests"]
        PyTest --> IntegrationTests["Integration Tests"]
        PyTest --> PropertyTests["Property-based Tests\n(Hypothesis)"]
        
        UnitTests --> TestComponents["Test Individual Components"]
        IntegrationTests --> TestPipeline["Test Processing Pipeline"]
        PropertyTests --> GenerateTestCases["Generate Test Cases"]
        
        Coverage["Coverage Tracking"] --> ReportCoverage["Coverage Reports"]
    end
```

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_logging.py:15-17](), [pyproject.toml:9-17]()

### 4.3 Example of a Test

The project uses fixtures, parameterization, and hypothesis for thorough testing. Here's a pattern often used in the tests:

1. Define fixtures for common test data
2. Use hypothesis to generate test cases
3. Use pytest's parameterization for edge cases
4. Test both expected success and failure conditions

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_logging.py:73-78](), [vermouth/tests/test_logging.py:22-25]()

## 5. Logging System

The project has a sophisticated logging system with custom adapters for formatting and categorizing log messages.

### 5.1 Logging Components

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class "PassingLoggerAdapter" {
        +process(msg, kwargs)
        +log(level, msg, *args, **kwargs)
    }
    
    class "StyleAdapter" {
        +log(level, msg, *args, **kwargs)
    }
    
    class "TypeAdapter" {
        +default_type: str
        +process(msg, kwargs)
    }
    
    class "CountingHandler" {
        +counts: defaultdict
        +handle(record)
        +number_of_counts_by(level, type)
    }
    
    PassingLoggerAdapter <|-- StyleAdapter
    PassingLoggerAdapter <|-- TypeAdapter
    logging.NullHandler <|-- CountingHandler
```

Sources: [vermouth/log_helpers.py:42-140](), [vermouth/log_helpers.py:177-228]()

### 5.2 Using the Logging System

When developing, use the `get_logger` function to obtain a logger:

```python
from vermouth.log_helpers import get_logger

# Get a logger for the current module
logger = get_logger(__name__)

# Log messages with type categorization
logger.info("Processing molecule %s", molecule_id, type="molecule")
logger.warning("Missing atom %s in residue %s", atom_name, residue_id, type="missing_atom")
```

Sources: [vermouth/log_helpers.py:231-242]()

## 6. Continuous Integration and Deployment

The project uses GitHub Actions for CI/CD with jobs for testing, linting, documentation building, and deployment.

### 6.1 CI/CD Pipeline Structure

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "On Push to master / Pull Request"
        PR["Push to master\nor Pull Request"]
        PR --> BuildTest["Build & Test"]
        PR --> Lint["Lint Code"]
        PR --> BuildDocs["Build Documentation"]
        
        BuildTest --> TestPy39["Test Python 3.9"]
        BuildTest --> TestPy310["Test Python 3.10"]
        BuildTest --> TestPy311["Test Python 3.11"]
        BuildTest --> TestPy312["Test Python 3.12"]
        
        TestPy39 --> CodeCov["Upload Coverage"]
        TestPy310 --> CodeCov
        TestPy311 --> CodeCov
        TestPy312 --> CodeCov
        
        BuildTest --> Deploy["Deploy to Test PyPI"]
        Lint --> Deploy
        BuildDocs --> Deploy
    end
    
    subgraph "On Release"
        Release["Create Release"]
        Release --> ReleaseBuild["Build & Test"]
        ReleaseBuild --> ReleaseDeploy["Deploy to PyPI"]
    end
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:1-154](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:1-151]()

### 6.2 CI Checks

Before merging a pull request, the following checks must pass:

1. **Tests**: All tests must pass on Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12
2. **Code Quality**: Vermouth must have a pylint score >= 8.0, martinize2 >= 9.0
3. **Documentation**: Documentation must build without warnings

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:87-92](), [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:114-117]()

## 7. Release Process

### 7.1 Version Management

The project uses PBR (Python Build Reasonableness) for version management, which derives version numbers from git tags.

### 7.2 Creating a Release

1. Create and push a git tag for the new version
2. Create a GitHub release
3. The CI/CD pipeline will automatically:
   - Run all tests
   - Build packages (wheel and source distribution)
   - Upload to PyPI

Sources: [setup.cfg:29-33](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:117-151]()

## 8. Additional Resources

- **Code Repository**: [GitHub Repo](https://github.com/marrink-lab/vermouth-martinize)
- **Documentation**: [ReadTheDocs](https://vermouth-martinize.readthedocs.io/)
- **Bug Reports**: [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/marrink-lab/vermouth-martinize/issues)
- **License**: Apache 2.0 (see LICENSE file in the repository)

Sources: [README.md:82-119]()

## 9. Contributing to the Project

Contributions are welcome as bug reports and pull requests. The project is under active development by the Marrink Lab at the University of Groningen.

Note that the decision about authorship on resulting academic papers is at the discretion of the core team.

Sources: [README.md:102-107](), [.zenodo.json:1-30]()

# Page: CI/CD Pipeline

# CI/CD Pipeline

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.github/workflows/deploy.yml](.github/workflows/deploy.yml)
- [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml](.github/workflows/run_tests.yml)
- [.zenodo.json](.zenodo.json)
- [LICENSE](LICENSE)
- [README.md](README.md)
- [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml)
- [setup.cfg](setup.cfg)
- [setup.py](setup.py)
- [vermouth/log_helpers.py](vermouth/log_helpers.py)
- [vermouth/tests/__init__.py](vermouth/tests/__init__.py)

This document describes the continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline implemented for the vermouth-martinize project. The pipeline automates testing, linting, documentation building, and package deployment processes, helping to maintain code quality and streamline the release process.

For information about writing tests, see [Testing Framework](#4.3.2).

## Overview of the CI/CD Pipeline

The vermouth-martinize project uses GitHub Actions to implement its CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline consists of two main workflows:

1. **Test workflow**: Runs on every push to the master branch and on pull requests
2. **Deploy workflow**: Runs when a new release is published

These workflows ensure that code changes are thoroughly tested before being merged and that releases are automatically published to PyPI.

### CI/CD Pipeline Diagram

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Code Changes"
        PR["Pull Request"]
        Push["Push to master"]
        Release["Release Published"]
    end

    subgraph "CI Pipeline"
        Tests["Run Tests"]
        Lint["Run Linting"]
        Docs["Build Documentation"]
    end

    subgraph "CD Pipeline"
        TestPyPI["Deploy to TestPyPI"]
        PyPI["Deploy to PyPI"]
    end

    PR --> Tests
    Push --> Tests
    Tests --> Lint
    Lint --> Docs
    Docs --> TestPyPI
    
    Release --> Tests
    Tests --> Lint
    Lint --> Docs
    Docs --> PyPI
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:6-10](), [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:120-121](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:6-8](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:118-119]()

## Continuous Integration Workflow

The CI workflow consists of four main jobs that run in sequence: `build` (tests), `lint`, `docs`, and `deploy` (to TestPyPI). This ensures that all aspects of the code are verified before deployment.

### Test Job

The test job is the core of the CI process. It:

1. Runs on multiple Python versions (3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12)
2. Installs DSSP (a dependency for secondary structure determination)
3. Installs the package and test requirements
4. Runs pytest with code coverage
5. Uploads coverage reports to Codecov

### Python Version Test Matrix

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Python Versions"
        PY39["Python 3.9"]
        PY310["Python 3.10"]
        PY311["Python 3.11"]
        PY312["Python 3.12"]
    end

    subgraph "Code Coverage"
        Coverage["Upload to Codecov"]
    end

    PY39 --> Coverage
    PY310 --> Coverage
    PY311 --> Coverage
    PY312 --> Coverage
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:21-32](), [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:54-67]()

### Lint Job

The lint job runs Pylint on the codebase with specific quality thresholds:

- The `vermouth` package must achieve at least an 8.0/10 score
- The `martinize2` script must achieve at least a 9.0/10 score

This ensures code quality is maintained across the project.

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:69-92]()

### Documentation Job

The documentation job builds the project documentation using Sphinx. This ensures that documentation is always up to date and properly formatted.

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:94-117]()

## Continuous Deployment Pipeline

The deployment pipeline has two paths:

1. **TestPyPI deployment** - Triggered by successful CI jobs on the master branch
2. **PyPI deployment** - Triggered when a new release is published

### TestPyPI Deployment

After the `build`, `lint`, and `docs` jobs succeed, the `deploy` job:

1. Builds a source distribution and wheel package
2. Publishes the package to TestPyPI

This allows for testing the package installation before an official release.

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:119-154]()

### PyPI Deployment

When a new release is published on GitHub, the deployment workflow:

1. Runs the same build, lint, and documentation jobs as the test workflow
2. Builds a source distribution and wheel package
3. Publishes the package to the official PyPI

Sources: [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:1-151]()

### Deployment Workflow Diagram

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Trigger"
        Release["GitHub Release"]
    end

    subgraph "Validation Jobs"
        Build["Run Tests on Multiple Python Versions"]
        Lint["Run Pylint"]
        Docs["Build Documentation"]
    end

    subgraph "Package Building"
        Checkout["Checkout Repository"]
        SetupPython["Setup Python"]
        InstallDeps["Install Dependencies"]
        BuildPackage["Build Source and Wheel"]
    end

    subgraph "Publication"
        PublishPyPI["Publish to PyPI"]
    end

    Release --> Build
    Build --> Lint
    Lint --> Docs
    Docs --> Checkout
    Checkout --> SetupPython
    SetupPython --> InstallDeps
    InstallDeps --> BuildPackage
    BuildPackage --> PublishPyPI
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:118-151]()

## GitHub Actions Configuration

The CI/CD pipeline is configured using GitHub Actions YAML files located in the `.github/workflows` directory.

### Workflow Triggers

- **Test workflow** (`run_tests.yml`): Triggered on pushes to the master branch and on pull requests to the master branch
- **Deploy workflow** (`deploy.yml`): Triggered when a new release is published

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:6-10](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:6-8]()

### Environment Variables

Both workflows use the following environment variables:

- `VERMOUTH_TEST_DSSP`: Set to "mkdssp" to specify the DSSP executable
- `SKIP_GENERATE_AUTHORS`: Set to 1 to skip author generation during build
- `SKIP_WRITE_GIT_CHANGELOG`: Set to 1 to skip changelog generation during build

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:12-15](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:10-13]()

## Package Building and Publishing Process

### Package Building Tools

The project uses the following tools for package building:

- **PBR (Python Build Reasonableness)**: Handles versioning based on git tags
- **setuptools**: Handles package metadata and dependencies
- **build**: Modern Python package builder

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    GitRepo["Git Repository"] --> PBR["Python Build Reasonableness (PBR)"]
    SetupCFG["setup.cfg"] --> PBR
    PyProject["pyproject.toml"] --> PBR
    
    PBR --> BuildModule["build module"]
    BuildModule --> SDist["Source Distribution (.tar.gz)"]
    BuildModule --> Wheel["Wheel Distribution (.whl)"]
    
    SDist --> PyPI["PyPI or TestPyPI"]
    Wheel --> PyPI
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml:1-8](), [setup.cfg:1-48](), [setup.py:1-31]()

### Package Configuration

The package metadata and build configuration are defined in several files:

- **setup.cfg**: Contains package metadata, dependencies, and classifiers
- **pyproject.toml**: Defines build system requirements
- **setup.py**: Handles package data files and script installation

#### Key Configuration Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| setup.cfg | Package metadata, dependencies, Python version compatibility |
| pyproject.toml | Build system requirements, pytest configuration, coverage settings |
| setup.py | Package data inclusion, script installation |

Sources: [setup.cfg:1-48](), [pyproject.toml:1-17](), [setup.py:1-31]()

## CI Badges and Status Indicators

The project uses several badges in its README to indicate the status of various CI aspects:

- GitHub Actions build status
- Codecov code coverage
- Documentation status
- DOI for citing the project
- arXiv paper reference

These badges provide quick visibility into the project's health and status.

Sources: [README.md:1-8]()

## Additional CI/CD Considerations

### Code Coverage

Code coverage tracking is implemented through the coverage.py tool and integrated with Codecov. This helps maintain and improve test coverage over time.

The coverage configuration in `pyproject.toml` specifies:
- Branch coverage is enabled
- Certain directories like tests and redistributed code are excluded from coverage reports

Sources: [pyproject.toml:14-17](), [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:54-67](), [.github/workflows/deploy.yml:52-65]()

### Documentation Generation

Documentation is built using Sphinx with the following settings:
- Source directory: `doc/source`
- Build directory: `doc/build`
- Warnings are treated as errors
- HTML is the primary builder format

Sources: [setup.cfg:44-48](), [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:94-117]()

# Page: Testing Framework

# Testing Framework

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

This document describes the testing framework used in the Vermouth-Martinize project. It outlines the tools, patterns, and practices used for testing the codebase, as well as how to write effective tests. For information on the CI/CD pipeline that runs these tests, see [CI/CD Pipeline](#4.3.1).

## Overview

The Vermouth-Martinize project uses a comprehensive testing approach based on pytest, with additional tools for coverage analysis, property-based testing, and code quality checking. Tests are an integral part of the development workflow and are automatically run on all pull requests and commits to the master branch.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Test Types"
        UnitTests["Unit Tests"]
        ParameterizedTests["Parameterized Tests"]
        PropertyTests["Property-Based Tests"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Testing Tools"
        Pytest["pytest"]
        Coverage["coverage.py"]
        Hypothesis["hypothesis"]
        Pylint["pylint"]
    end
    
    subgraph "CI Integration"
        GithubActions["GitHub Actions"]
        CodeCov["Codecov"]
    end
    
    UnitTests --> Pytest
    ParameterizedTests --> Pytest
    PropertyTests --> Hypothesis
    Hypothesis --> Pytest
    
    Pytest --> Coverage
    Coverage --> CodeCov
    
    Pytest --> GithubActions
    Pylint --> GithubActions
    CodeCov --> GithubActions
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:54-58](), [pyproject.toml:9-16]()

## Test Organization and Structure

Tests in the Vermouth-Martinize project follow a consistent organization pattern.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class "Project Structure" {
        vermouth/
        vermouth/tests/
        vermouth/tests/test_*.py
        vermouth/tests/helper_functions.py
        vermouth/tests/datafiles/
    }
    
    class "Test File Structure" {
        imports
        fixtures
        test_functions
        helper_functions
    }
    
    class "Test Function" {
        +test_name()
        +@pytest.mark.parametrize()
        +assertions
    }
    
    "Project Structure" --> "Test File Structure": contains
    "Test File Structure" --> "Test Function": contains
```

All tests are located in the `vermouth/tests/` directory with filenames following the pattern `test_*.py`. Helper functions and common fixtures are defined in `helper_functions.py`.

Sources: [pyproject.toml:9-12](), [vermouth/tests/helper_functions.py:15-235]()

## Testing Tools and Configuration

### pytest

The primary testing framework used is pytest. It's configured in the project's `pyproject.toml` file:

```toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--import-mode=importlib"
testpaths = ["vermouth/tests"]
python_files = "test_*.py"
```

### Coverage

Code coverage measurement is performed using coverage.py, which is integrated with pytest in the CI pipeline. The configuration in `pyproject.toml` specifies which files to include/exclude:

```toml
[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true
omit = ["vermouth/tests/*", "vermouth/redistributed/*", '*/bin/pytest']
source_pkgs = ["vermouth"]
```

### Pylint

Code quality is enforced using pylint with different thresholds for different parts of the codebase:

- Vermouth library: minimum score of 8.0
- martinize2 command-line tool: minimum score of 9.0

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:88-91](), [pyproject.toml:9-16]()

## Writing Tests

### Basic Test Structure

Tests in the Vermouth-Martinize project typically follow this structure:

```python
# Import required modules
import pytest
import vermouth

# Define test function
def test_function_name():
    # Set up test data
    input_data = ...
    
    # Call the function under test
    result = vermouth.module.function(input_data)
    
    # Assert expected outcomes
    assert result == expected_result
```

### Using Fixtures

Fixtures are extensively used to set up test conditions and provide reusable test components:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Test Function"
        TestFunc["test_function(fixture1, fixture2)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Fixtures"
        Fixture1["@pytest.fixture\ndef fixture1()"]
        Fixture2["@pytest.fixture\ndef fixture2(fixture1)"]
    end
    
    Fixture1 --> Fixture2
    Fixture2 --> TestFunc
    Fixture1 --> TestFunc
```

Example fixtures are defined in test files like `test_repair_graph.py`, where fixtures create test systems with specific characteristics that can be reused across multiple tests.

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_repair_graph.py:161-186]()

### Parameterized Testing

Many tests use parameterization to run the same test logic with different input values:

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize('input_data, expected_output', [
    (input1, output1),
    (input2, output2),
    # ...more test cases
])
def test_something(input_data, expected_output):
    result = function_under_test(input_data)
    assert result == expected_output
```

This approach reduces code duplication and makes it easy to add more test cases.

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_graph_utils.py:46-68](), [vermouth/tests/test_repair_graph.py:190-200]()

### Property-Based Testing with Hypothesis

For some components, especially those with complex logic like graph algorithms, property-based testing with the Hypothesis library is used:

```python
@given(graph_builder(...))
def test_property(graph):
    # Test that some property holds for any valid graph
    assert property_function(graph)
```

This is particularly evident in the ISMAGS algorithm tests, where randomly generated graphs are used to test isomorphism properties.

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_ismags.py:152-158]()

## Test Helper Functions

The project includes several helper functions to simplify test writing:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class "Helper Functions" {
        +make_into_set(iter_of_dict)
        +equal_graphs(g1, g2, node_attrs, edge_attrs)
        +basic_molecule(node_data, edge_data)
        +create_sys_all_attrs(...)
        +test_molecule()
    }
    
    class "Test Functions" {
        +test_something(fixture)
    }
    
    "Helper Functions" --> "Test Functions": used by
```

Key helper functions include:

- `make_into_set()`: Converts iterables of dictionaries to sets for comparison
- `equal_graphs()`: Compares graph isomorphism with attribute matching
- `basic_molecule()`: Creates a simple molecule from node and edge data
- Various fixtures that provide ready-to-use molecular structures

Sources: [vermouth/tests/helper_functions.py:28-34](), [vermouth/tests/helper_functions.py:36-65](), [vermouth/tests/helper_functions.py:88-153]()

## CI/CD Integration

Tests are integrated into the CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PushOrPR["Push to master\nor Pull Request"] --> Build["Build Job"]
    
    subgraph "Build Job"
        Pytest["Run pytest"]
        CodeCov["Upload to Codecov"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Lint Job"
        Pylint["Run pylint"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Docs Job"
        Sphinx["Build Sphinx docs"]
    end
    
    Build --> Deploy["Deploy Job"]
    Lint --> Deploy
    Docs --> Deploy
    
    PushOrPR --> Lint
    PushOrPR --> Docs
```

The pipeline runs tests on multiple Python versions (3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12) to ensure compatibility. Code coverage is measured during test execution and uploaded to Codecov for tracking and visualization.

Sources: [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:18-33](), [.github/workflows/run_tests.yml:54-67]()

## Test Patterns and Best Practices

### Testing Graph Operations

Since Vermouth-Martinize heavily relies on graph operations, many tests follow patterns for testing graph isomorphism, attribute matching, and transformation correctness:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Graph Testing Pattern"
        Input["Create Input Graph"] --> Operation["Apply Operation"]
        Operation --> Verification["Verify Output Graph"]
        Verification --> IsomorphismCheck["Check Graph Isomorphism"]
        Verification --> AttributeCheck["Check Node/Edge Attributes"]
    end
```

This pattern can be seen in tests for graph repairs, modifications, and transformations.

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_repair_graph.py:402-405](), [vermouth/tests/test_graph_utils.py:434-442]()

### Testing Parsers

For testing file parsers (like those for ITP and FF files), the pattern typically involves:

1. Create a string containing the file content
2. Parse the string 
3. Check that the resulting data structure matches expectations

This approach is used in tests like `test_itp_files.py` and `test_ff_files.py`.

Sources: [vermouth/tests/test_itp_files.py:25-35](), [vermouth/tests/test_ff_files.py:27-37]()

## Adding New Tests

When adding new functionality, follow these steps to add tests:

1. Create a new test file in `vermouth/tests/` if testing a new module
2. Use existing test patterns and fixtures where applicable
3. Write parameterized tests to cover multiple input cases
4. Use property-based testing for algorithms with complex properties
5. Ensure your tests have good coverage of edge cases
6. Use meaningful test names that describe what is being tested

# Tutorials

This page provides practical guides for using martinize2 in various scenarios. It serves as a starting point for both new and experienced users who want to learn how to effectively use martinize2 for coarse-graining molecular structures. These tutorials cover basic usage as well as more advanced features like applying elastic networks, Go models, water biasing, and making mutations or modifications to proteins during the coarse-graining process.

## Tutorial Overview

The following diagram shows the general workflow of martinize2 and the key features covered in these tutorials:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input Structure\n(PDB/GRO/CIF)"] --> DSSP["Secondary Structure\nAssignment"]
    DSSP --> CG["Coarse-Graining"]
    CG --> Outputs["Output Files\n(topology, structure)"]
    
    subgraph "Structure Stabilization"
        EN["Elastic Network"]
        GO["Go Model"]
        WB["Water Biasing"]
    end
    
    CG --> EN
    CG --> GO
    CG --> WB
    
    subgraph "Protein Modifications"
        MUT["Mutations"]
        MOD["Modifications"]
    end
    
    Input --> MUT
    Input --> MOD
    MUT --> CG
    MOD --> CG
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:1-1059](), [vermouth/dssp/dssp.py:1-150]()

## Basic Usage

The most basic use of martinize2 converts an atomistic protein structure to a coarse-grained model:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb
```

This command takes a protein PDB file as input (`-f`), produces a GROMACS topology file (`-o`), and outputs the coarse-grained structure in PDB format (`-x`). By default, martinize2 uses the Martini 3 force field.

### Force Field Selection

You can select different force fields using the `-ff` option:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -ff martini22
```

To see all available force fields:

```
martinize2 -list-ff
```

### Secondary Structure Considerations

For realistic coarse-grained models, you need to account for secondary structure:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:871-971](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:1-57]()

## Secondary Structure Handling

Secondary structure determination is critical for proper coarse-graining of proteins. Martinize2 offers several options:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input PDB"] --> Choose["Choose SS Method"]
    
    Choose -->|"Option 1"| DSSP["DSSP\nAutomatic detection"]
    Choose -->|"Option 2"| Manual["Manual Assignment\n(-ss flag)"]
    Choose -->|"Option 3"| Collagen["Collagen Parameters\n(-collagen)"]
    
    DSSP --> DSS1["Use local DSSP executable\n(-dssp /path/to/dssp)"]
    DSSP --> DSS2["Use MDTraj implementation\n(-dssp)"]
    
    Manual --> MAN1["Full sequence\n(-ss HHHEEEECCCC)"]
    Manual --> MAN2["Single letter\n(-ss H)"]
    
    DSS1 --> Convert["Convert to Martini SS codes"]
    DSS2 --> Convert
    MAN1 --> Convert
    MAN2 --> Convert
    Collagen --> Convert
    
    Convert --> CG["Apply to CG model"]
```

### Using DSSP

DSSP automatically determines secondary structure from atomic coordinates:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp
```

If you have a local DSSP executable:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp /path/to/dssp
```

### Manual Assignment

To manually specify secondary structure:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -ss HHHEEEECCCC
```

This requires one character per residue in the protein. Alternatively, to set all residues to the same secondary structure:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -ss H
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:442-461](), [vermouth/dssp/dssp.py:384-446](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:26-83]()

## Elastic Networks

Elastic networks help maintain protein structure by adding harmonic bonds between backbone beads within a cutoff distance.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CG["Coarse-Grained Structure"] --> Apply["Apply Elastic Network\n(-elastic)"]
    Apply --> Customize["Customize Network Parameters"]
    
    Customize --> Cutoff["Distance Cutoffs\n(-el lower, -eu upper)"]
    Customize --> Force["Force Constant\n(-ef)"]
    Customize --> Decay["Decay Function\n(-ea factor, -ep power)"]
    Customize --> Unit["Structural Unit\n(-eunit)"]
    
    Decay --> DecayEq["decay = e^(- f * ((x - l) ^ p))"]
    
    Cutoff --> Result["Final Elastic Network"]
    Force --> Result
    DecayEq --> Result
    Unit --> Result
```

To add a basic elastic network:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -elastic
```

### Customizing Elastic Networks

You can customize various aspects of the elastic network:

- Force constant: `-ef 700` (default: 700 kJ/mol/nm²)
- Distance cutoffs: `-el 0` (lower bound, default: 0) and `-eu 0.9` (upper bound, default: 0.9 nm)
- Decay parameters: `-ea` (decay factor) and `-ep` (decay power)
- Structural unit: `-eunit molecule|chain|all|<resid ranges>`

Example with custom parameters:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -elastic -ef 500 -el 0.5 -eu 1.2 -ea 0.5 -ep 2
```

### Structural Units

By default, elastic bonds are only created within each molecule. To change this:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -elastic -eunit chain
```

To specify regions where elastic bonds should be applied:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -elastic -eunit 1:100,150:200
```

This creates elastic bonds within residues 1-100 and 150-200, but not between them.

Sources: [bin/martinize2:472-546](), [doc/source/tutorials/elastic_networks.rst:1-136]()

## Go Models

Go models maintain protein structure through non-bonded interactions based on native contacts. Martinize2 implements this using virtual sites placed on backbone beads.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input Structure"] --> CM["Contact Map Generation"]
    
    CM --> CMO1["Option 1: Calculate in martinize2\n(-go)"]
    CM --> CMO2["Option 2: Use server-generated map\n(-go contact_map.out)"]
    
    CMO1 --> VS["Generate Virtual Sites\non backbone beads"]
    CMO2 --> VS
    
    VS --> Filter["Filter Contacts\n(-go-low, -go-up, -go-res-dist)"]
    
    Filter --> Files["Generate Output Files"]
    Files --> AT["go_atomtypes.itp"]
    Files --> NB["go_nbparams.itp"]
    
    AT --> Setup["Setup in Topology"]
    NB --> Setup
```

To add a Go model calculated on-the-fly:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -go
```

To use a pre-calculated contact map:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -go contact_map.out
```

### Customizing Go Models

You can customize Go model parameters:

- Interaction strength: `-go-eps 9.414` (default: 9.414 kJ/mol)
- Distance cutoffs: `-go-low 0.3` (minimum, default: 0.3 nm) and `-go-up 1.1` (maximum, default: 1.1 nm)
- Residue distance cutoff: `-go-res-dist 3` (default: 3 residues)
- Backbone bead name: `-go-backbone BB` (default: BB)
- Virtual site atom name: `-go-atomname CA` (default: CA)

Example with custom parameters:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -go -go-eps 7.5 -go-low 0.4 -go-up 1.0
```

### Using Go Models in Simulations

The Go model generates two additional files:
1. `go_atomtypes.itp`: Defines virtual site atom types
2. `go_nbparams.itp`: Defines non-bonded interactions between virtual sites

To use these in GROMACS, you need to include them in your force field file and activate them with a preprocessor directive:

```
#ifdef GO_VIRT
#include "go_atomtypes.itp"
#endif

[nonbond_params]
...

#ifdef GO_VIRT
#include "go_nbparams.itp"
#endif
```

Then in your topology file, add `#define GO_VIRT` to activate the Go model.

Sources: [bin/martinize2:547-608](), [doc/source/tutorials/go_models.rst:1-184]()

## Water Biasing

Water biasing adjusts the interaction between proteins and water based on secondary structure elements or intrinsically disordered regions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CG["Coarse-Grained Structure"] --> WB["Apply Water Bias\n(-water-bias)"]
    WB --> SS["Secondary Structure-Based Bias\n(-water-bias-eps)"]
    WB --> IDR["Intrinsically Disordered Regions\n(-id-regions)"]
    
    SS --> SSP["Set Bias per SS type\n(H:3.6 C:2.1)"]
    IDR --> IDRTune["Enable IDR Tuning\n(-idr-tune)"]
    IDR --> IDRBias["Set IDR Water Bias\n(-water-bias-eps idr:2.1)"]
    
    SSP --> NBINT["Non-bonded Interactions\nwith Water"]
    IDRTune --> BONDED["IDR-specific\nBonded Parameters"]
    IDRBias --> NBINT
    
    NBINT --> Files["Generate Output Files"]
    BONDED --> Files
```

To apply water bias based on secondary structure:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -water-bias -water-bias-eps H:3.6 C:2.1
```

This creates additional interactions between water and the backbone virtual sites, with an epsilon of 3.6 kJ/mol for helices and 2.1 kJ/mol for coils.

### Intrinsically Disordered Regions

To specify and bias intrinsically disordered regions:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -id-regions 1:10 65:92 -idr-tune -water-bias -water-bias-eps idr:2.1
```

This:
1. Identifies residues 1-10 and 65-92 as disordered regions
2. Applies special bonded parameters with `-idr-tune`
3. Adds water bias with strength 2.1 kJ/mol for these regions

Sources: [bin/martinize2:610-646](), [vermouth/processors/annotate_idrs.py:1-114](), [doc/source/tutorials/water_biasing.rst:1-73]()

## Mutations and Modifications

Martinize2 allows you to apply mutations and modifications to proteins during coarse-graining.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input Structure"] --> Syntax["Mutation/Modification Syntax\n<chain>-<resname><resid>:<new resname>"]
    
    Syntax --> MUT["Mutations\n(-mutate)"]
    Syntax --> MOD["Modifications\n(-modify)"]
    
    MUT --> MT1["Single Residue\nA-PHE45:ALA"]
    MUT --> MT2["All Residues of Type\nARG:LYS"]
    MUT --> MT3["Chain-Specific\nB-ARG:LYS"]
    
    MOD --> MD1["Terminal Modifications\n(-nter, -cter)"]
    MOD --> MD2["Neutral Termini\n(-nt)"]
    MOD --> MD3["Specific Modifications\nA-ASP45:ASP0"]
    
    MT1 --> CG["Apply During Coarse-Graining"]
    MT2 --> CG
    MT3 --> CG
    MD1 --> CG
    MD2 --> CG
    MD3 --> CG
```

### Mutations

To mutate a specific residue:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -mutate A-PHE45:ALA
```

To mutate all residues of a specific type:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -mutate ARG:LYS
```

To mutate residues only on a specific chain:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -mutate B-ARG:LYS
```

### Modifications

To modify termini:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -nter NH2-ter -cter COOH-ter
```

To use neutral termini (shorthand):

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -nt
```

To apply specific modifications:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -modify A-ASP45:ASP0
```

**Note:** While martinize2 can apply mutations and modifications to the topology, it does not create actual coordinates for new atoms. These may appear as "NaN" in the output structure file.

Sources: [bin/martinize2:649-730](), [doc/source/tutorials/mutations_and_modifications.rst:1-54]()

## Additional Features

### Cysteine Bridges

Martinize2 can automatically detect and create cysteine bridges:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -cys auto
```

You can also specify a distance cutoff:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -cys 0.5
```

### Molecule Naming

By default, molecules are named `molecule_0`, `molecule_1`, etc. To change this:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -name myprotein
```

This will name the molecules `myprotein_0`, `myprotein_1`, etc., which is particularly important when using Go models to ensure unique atom names.

### Side Chain Fixing

From version 0.12.0 onward, side chain fixing is applied automatically. For earlier versions, use:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -scfix
```

To disable side chain fixing:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp -noscfix
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:664-671](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:89-152]()

---

# Basic Usage

This document provides a step-by-step guide for using martinize2, a tool for converting atomistic molecular structures to coarse-grained models using the Martini force field. It covers the basic command-line interface, essential flags, and common usage scenarios. For more advanced features like elastic networks and Go models, see [Adding Elastic Networks](#5.2) and [Working with Go Models](#5.3).

## Martinize2 Overview

Martinize2 is a command-line tool that converts atomistic structures (usually proteins) into coarse-grained models compatible with the Martini force field. The basic workflow involves:

1. Reading an input structure file (PDB, GRO, or CIF)
2. Processing the structure (repairing, mapping to coarse-grained representation)
3. Writing output files (topology and structure) ready for simulation

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Basic Workflow"
        direction LR
        A["Input File\n(.pdb/.gro/.cif)"] --> B["martinize2"]
        B --> C["CG Structure\n(.pdb)"]
        B --> D["Topology Files\n(.top/.itp)"]
    end
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:1-1100]()

## Command-Line Basics

The most minimal command to convert a protein to a coarse-grained representation:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb
```

This command:
- Reads an atomistic structure from `protein.pdb`
- Produces a coarse-grained structure in `cg_protein.pdb`
- Generates topology files starting with `topol.top`

By default, martinize2 uses the Martini 3.0.0.1 force field. To view available force fields:

```
martinize2 -list-ff
```

To use a specific force field:

```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -ff martini22
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:294-399](), [bin/martinize2:806-845](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:1-19]()

## Input/Output File Structure

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Input Files"
        PDB["PDB File\n(.pdb)"]
        GRO["GRO File\n(.gro)"]
        CIF["CIF File\n(.cif)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "martinize2"
        direction LR
        READ["Read Input\nPDBInput/GROInput/CIFInput"]
        PROCESS["Process\nMakeBonds → RepairGraph → DoMapping → DoLinks"]
        WRITE["Write Output"]
        
        READ --> PROCESS
        PROCESS --> WRITE
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Files"
        CG_PDB["Coarse-grained structure\n(.pdb)"]
        TOP["System topology\n(.top)"]
        ITP["Molecule parameters\n(.itp)"]
    end
    
    PDB --> READ
    GRO --> READ
    CIF --> READ
    
    WRITE --> CG_PDB
    WRITE --> TOP
    WRITE --> ITP
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:81-104](), [bin/martinize2:169-192](), [bin/martinize2:1000-1033]()

### Output Files Explanation:

- **Coarse-grained structure (.pdb)**: Contains the coordinates of coarse-grained beads
- **System topology (.top)**: Main GROMACS topology file that includes component molecules
- **Molecule parameters (.itp)**: Contains parameters for each molecule type (one per molecule by default)

## Secondary Structure Assignment

Martini requires secondary structure information to correctly parametrize proteins. There are three ways to provide this:

1. **Automatic using DSSP** (recommended):
   ```
   martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp
   ```
   
2. **Using an external DSSP executable**:
   ```
   martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp /path/to/dssp
   ```
   
3. **Manual assignment**:
   ```
   martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -ss HHHHHCCCCCEEEEE
   ```
   Where the string length must match the number of residues, or use a single letter (e.g., `-ss H`) to apply uniformly.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Input PDB"] --> CHOICE{"How to assign\nsecondary structure?"}
    CHOICE -->|"Automatic (-dssp)"| MDTRAJ["MDTraj DSSP"]
    CHOICE -->|"External (-dssp /path)"| DSSP["External DSSP"]
    CHOICE -->|"Manual (-ss)"| MANUAL["User-defined SS"]
    
    MDTRAJ --> SS["Secondary Structure Assigned"]
    DSSP --> SS
    MANUAL --> SS
    
    SS --> MARTINIZE["Continue martinize process"]
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:442-470](), [vermouth/dssp/dssp.py:560-645](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:20-85]()

## Essential Flags and Options

### Force Field Selection
- `-ff <name>`: Specify the force field (default: martini3001)
- `-from <name>`: Specify the input force field (default: charmm)
- `-ff-dir <path>`: Provide additional force field directory
- `-map-dir <path>`: Provide additional mapping directory

### Side Chain Fixing
Side chain fixing adds special bonded terms to ensure correct sampling of side chain dynamics:
- In martinize2 ≥ 0.12.0, side chain fixing is done automatically
- For older versions, use `-scfix` flag
- To disable, use `-noscfix`

### Cysteine Bridges
Martinize2 can identify and create disulfide bridges:
- `-cys auto`: Automatically detect bridges (default)
- `-cys <distance>`: Use custom distance cutoff in nm
- `-cys none`: Disable cysteine bridges

### Molecule Naming
- `-name <prefix>`: Set prefix for molecule names (default: molecule)
- `-sep`: Write separate topologies for identical chains

Sources: [bin/martinize2:387-414](), [bin/martinize2:649-670](), [bin/martinize2:957-974](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:89-165]()

## Processing Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    INPUT["Input Structure"] --> BONDS["MakeBonds\nCreate bonds based on distance/name"]
    BONDS --> REPAIR["RepairGraph\nFix missing atoms"]
    REPAIR --> CANON["CanonicalizeModifications\nStandardize residue modifications"]
    CANON --> MAPPING["DoMapping\nConvert to coarse-grained"]
    MAPPING --> AVERAGE["DoAverageBead\nAverage atomistic coordinates"]
    AVERAGE --> LINKS["DoLinks\nAdd bonds between residues"]
    LINKS --> DUMMIES["LocateChargeDummies\nPlace charge dummies if needed"]
    DUMMIES --> OUTPUT["Output Files"]
    
    style BONDS fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style REPAIR fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style CANON fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style MAPPING fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style AVERAGE fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style LINKS fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
    style DUMMIES fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333
```

Sources: [bin/martinize2:106-167](), [bin/martinize2:169-192](), [vermouth/processors/__init__.py:1-49]()

## Complete Example

Let's walk through a complete example converting an atomistic protein to a coarse-grained model:

1. **Basic conversion with automatic secondary structure detection**:
   ```
   martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -dssp
   ```

2. **Examining output files**:
   - `topol.top`: Main topology file that includes:
     - Force field parameters
     - Included molecule parameter files
     - System composition
   - `molecule_0.itp`: Molecule parameters including:
     - Atoms definition
     - Bonds, angles, dihedrals
     - Constraints
   - `cg_protein.pdb`: 3D structure with coarse-grained beads

3. **Building a simulation system** (outside of martinize2):
   - Add solvent, ions, etc. to your system
   - Set up an energy minimization and simulation with GROMACS

Sources: [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:1-185]()

## Common Options Table

| Flag | Description | Default | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|---------|
| `-f` | Input structure file | Required | `-f protein.pdb` |
| `-o` | Output topology file | Required | `-o topol.top` |
| `-x` | Output coarse-grained structure | Optional | `-x cg_protein.pdb` |
| `-ff` | Target force field | martini3001 | `-ff martini22` |
| `-dssp` | Use DSSP for secondary structure | - | `-dssp` or `-dssp /path/to/dssp` |
| `-ss` | Manual secondary structure | - | `-ss HHHHEEEECCCC` |
| `-name` | Molecule name prefix | molecule | `-name Protein_A` |
| `-cys` | Cysteine bridge detection | auto | `-cys 0.5` |
| `-ignore` | Ignore residues | - | `-ignore HOH,SOL` |
| `-scfix` | Apply side chain corrections | True (v≥0.12) | Not needed in newer versions |
| `-noscfix` | Disable side chain corrections | - | `-noscfix` |

Sources: [bin/martinize2:293-747]()

## Troubleshooting

### Handling Warnings
Martinize2 issues warnings when it encounters issues. You can control how many warnings are allowed:
```
martinize2 -f protein.pdb -o topol.top -x cg_protein.pdb -maxwarn 10
```

### Missing Atoms
If your input structure has missing atoms, martinize2 will try to repair them. However, for significant gaps, you may need to fix your input structure using external tools.

### Secondary Structure Assignment
If DSSP fails or gives unexpected results, try manually specifying the secondary structure with `-ss`.

Sources: [bin/martinize2:769-780](), [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:170-185]()

## Citations

Martinize2 collects paper citation information based on the features used. The citations are printed at the end of execution and included in the output topology files. Please cite all the papers mentioned to give proper credit to the authors.

Sources: [doc/source/tutorials/basic_usage.rst:173-185]()

# Adding Elastic Networks

<details>
